title: VOID PVP — window.void bridge surface
description: The single `window.void` object that joins the Java mod and the in-game React app, as specified in PVP_ARCHITECTURE.md §6.5. Java to JS is push, delivered through `void.on(event, handler)` and batched once per frame; JS to Java is a direct call. The bridge is in-process (Ultralight lives inside the JVM, §6.2), so calls are synchronous and return real applied state -- there is no ack, no optimistic UI and no request id. This file therefore does not describe a transport; it describes, per event, the shape of the payload handed to the handler, and per call, the positional `params` and the `returns` value. An instance of this schema is one enveloped event, call or call result, which is exactly the form the browser `?debug` harness of §9 records and replays against a fake window.void. Payloads are additionalProperties:false: unlike protocol.json this surface is not forward-compatible across versions, because the mod JAR embeds the UI bundle and the two always ship as one binary. The channel list below is the whole contract and both shims close over it: `on` returns a no-op subscription for a name it does not know and `__emit` drops an envelope whose channel has no list, so a channel Java pushes and this file does not declare is lost in total silence. That is how `session` went missing between Java and the page the first time, and why it is written down here now.

oneOf.description: A Java to JS event push.
The value a JS to Java call returned.

event_name.title: Event name
event_name.description: The fourteen channels Java pushes on. Closed set; `void.on` with any other name is a programming error — and, because both shims close their channel list over this enum, silently a no-op rather than a throw.

call_name.title: Call name
call_name.description: The twenty-one methods JS may call on `window.void`. Closed set.

event.title: Event
event.description: One push from Java to JS, enveloped as {e, payload}. In the real bridge the envelope does not exist on the wire: `payload` is the single argument the `void.on(e, handler)` handler receives.

oneOf.description: The loadout library changed, or was delivered for the first time.
One mod setting changed outside the UI's own call.
Who is playing. Pushed once, on the first paint.
A key bound to one mod asked that mod to do something.
A short notice for the player.
What the local player wears and owns.
The local player's emote started or ended.

payload.description: The whole library, in library order.
The mod, the key and the value Java stored.
Whether the menu is now open.
Which mod, and what its key asked for.
The sidebar as vanilla would draw it.

keys_payload.title: keys payload
keys_payload.description: Edge-triggered key state, pushed only when a key changes, from `KeyBinding.setKeyBindState` (§6.6). Each field is 0 for released and 1 for pressed -- integers, not booleans, so the UI can index a sprite row and so that a future analogue axis fits without a shape change. In HUD mode Ultralight receives no input events at all (§6.3); this event is how the player's keys reach the UI, as data. The renderer must touch only the changed key's node (§9).

lmb.description: Left mouse button state. The CPS mod derives clicks per second from the rising edges of this field (§3).

tick_payload.title: tick payload
tick_payload.description: All per-tick telemetry, coalesced into one push per game tick, i.e. 20 Hz (§6.6). Every HUD mod other than keystrokes and CPS reads from this. Fields whose sensor has nothing to report are omitted rather than sent as null, so a handler must treat an absent field as unchanged. Every field is optional and absent means unchanged; the sensor coalesces, because an uncoalesced field costs a full-surface Ultralight repaint (`TickCoalescer`'s header has the measurements).

ping.description: Round-trip time in milliseconds from the player's own `NetworkPlayerInfo.responseTime`; -1 when unknown, such as in singleplayer or before the player list arrives.

armor.description: Worn armor and, when enabled, the held item. Present only on the ticks where durability or the equipped set changed.

fx.description: Active potion effects. Present only on the ticks where the effect set changed.

saturation.description: Food saturation, the hidden half of the hunger bar. Vanilla never draws it and it is what decides whether you regenerate, which is why every competing client ships a readout for it. Value-checked only, not rate-limited: it moves on eating and on exertion, not every tick.

held_count.description: Stack size of the held item, for the item counter. Absent when the hand is empty — a count of 0 and an empty hand are different states, and the widget draws nothing rather than a zero. Value-checked; a stack size changes on use, not on a clock.

speed.description: Horizontal ground speed in blocks per second, for the momentum readout. Horizontal on purpose: falling is not momentum a player is steering, and including it would make the number spike on every drop. Rounded to 2 dp at the sensor and rate-limited, because it changes every tick while moving and an uncoalesced field costs a full-surface repaint (see `TickCoalescer`'s header).

memory.description: JVM heap, for the memory readout. Rate-limited hard: it changes constantly, nobody reads it twenty times a second, and it is the field most able to undo the coalescing this payload exists for.

hits.description: Monotonic hit counters, and the raw material for the combo counter. NOT the combo itself: a combo is a count with a *timeout policy* on it, and the timeout is a mod setting, so deriving it here would put a UI policy in the sensor. `cps` already sets that precedent — `mods.json` records that it is derived entirely in JS from click edges and has no Java sensor. Counters rather than hit *events* because an event lost to a dropped tick leaves the combo wrong forever, whereas a counter that jumps by two is still exactly right.

dealt.description: Attacks the player has landed since the session began. Monotonic; never reset on the wire.

taken.description: Times the player has been hit since the session began. Monotonic. A combo breaks when this moves, which is why it is sent rather than derived from health.

swings.description: Times `MinecraftClient.doAttack` has run since the session began, whatever it hit. Monotonic. A left click the game swallowed (1.8's miss delay, a screen open) never reaches `doAttack`, so the difference between this and the mouse edges on `keys` is exactly the cancelled clicks; `cps.ignore_cancelled` counts these instead of the edges. Optional so a sensor that predates it still validates.

counts.description: Inventory-wide item counts, for the Item counter's named `track` values and the Potion counter. Every key is the total across the 36 main inventory slots (hotbar included, armour and the cursor stack excluded). `held_total` is every stack matching the held item, same item and same variant, and is absent with an empty hand; `wool` is every colour together; `health_potion` is splash potions of Healing I and II; `soup` is mushroom stew. Sent whole whenever any key changes and omitted otherwise, like `armor`: an absent field means unchanged. Value-checked, never rate-limited, because a count changes on use and pickup rather than on a clock.

reach.description: The reach of the most recent landed attack, for the Reach display. Measured on the client when the attack is sent: from the eye position interpolated to the frame the crosshair ray was cast on, to the point where that ray met the target's hitbox. `n` counts measured attacks and is monotonic, so two hits at the same distance are still two readings; the page keeps the history it averages over. Absent until the first measured attack, and after that sent only on the tick a new one lands.

blocks.description: Eye-to-hit-point distance in blocks, rounded to 3 decimals.

n.description: Measured attacks since the session began. Monotonic.

position.title: Position
position.description: Player position and yaw from `EntityPlayerSP`, read once per tick. Pitch is deliberately absent: no mod in §3 uses it.

y.description: World Y in blocks, feet level.

yaw.description: Facing in degrees, normalised to [-180, 180). The coordinates mod derives the cardinal direction from this.

armor_slot.title: Armor slot
armor_slot.description: One equipment slot from `InventoryPlayer.armorInventory`, or the held item when the armor status mod has `show_held_item` on.

item.description: Minecraft item id such as `diamond_chestplate`, or null when the slot is empty.

damage.description: Damage taken by the item. 0 is undamaged.

max_damage.description: Maximum durability of the item; 0 for items that do not take damage.

count.description: Stack size, relevant only for the held slot.

enchanted.description: Whether the item has any enchantment, so the UI can draw the glint treatment.

id.description: Numeric potion id as used by 1.8.9.

name.description: Unlocalised effect name such as `potion.moveSpeed`, for the UI to map to a label and icon.

amplifier.description: Amplifier level, 0-based: 0 renders as I, 1 as II.

duration_ms.description: Remaining duration in milliseconds, converted from ticks by the sensor so the UI never needs to know the tick rate.

ambient.description: Whether the effect comes from an ambient source such as a beacon; hidden when `hide_ambient` is set.

server_payload.title: server payload
server_payload.description: Pushed on connect and disconnect (§6.6). The same information also goes to Rust as the `server` protocol message.

host.description: Hostname of the server without port; empty string on disconnect.

connected.description: True on connect, false on disconnect.

loadout_payload.title: loadout payload
loadout_payload.description: The full active loadout. Pushed once on `hello` and again on every switch, whether the switch came from Rust, from the tray, from the L key or from `void.switchLoadout` (§6.5). The UI store treats this as a whole-state replacement.

loadouts_payload.title: loadouts payload
loadouts_payload.description: Every loadout in the library, in full and in library order, including the active one — exactly what Rust sent in `init.loadouts`. Pushed once on `init` and again whenever the library changes, so the in-game Loadouts frame (Figma 244:1130) can list and compare loadouts, and the quick palette can offer `Turn on in <other> loadout`, without a bridge accessor and without waiting to observe a `loadout` event per entry. Whole-state replacement, like `loadout`.

setting_payload.title: setting payload
setting_payload.description: One mod setting Java changed on its own — an in-game hotkey toggling a mod (the `keystrokes.keybind` overlay key), or a launcher-side `state` echo. It is *not* pushed for a change the page itself made through `setModSetting`: that call already returned the stored value, and re-pushing it would fight the control the player is holding. The UI applies it exactly as it applies the return value of `setModSetting`, so a whole-loadout replacement is not needed for a one-key change.

id.description: Which mod changed. Any of the 13.

key.description: Name of the setting, a property of that mod's settings sub-schema. `on` included.

value.description: The value Java stored, after clamping — the same value `setModSetting` would have returned.

menu_payload.title: menu payload
menu_payload.description: True when VoidMenuScreen opened, false when it closed. The React app draws the HUD layer and the menu layer into the same Ultralight view (§6.2); this flag is how it decides which is visible.

session_payload.title: session payload
session_payload.description: Who is playing: the account the launcher signed in with, as Java already knows it from the JVM arguments it was spawned with. Pushed on `pushWholeState()` — first paint, a launcher `init`, and a reloaded document (design/rendering-invariants.md §9a) — and never again in between: the account cannot change while the game runs. The About screen prints it, and the HUD greets by name.

name.description: The player's Minecraft name, as the launcher signed in.

uuid.description: The account uuid. For an offline launch this is the uuid derived from the name, not a Mojang one.

kind.description: `microsoft` for a signed-in Xbox account; `offline` when the uuid is the one an offline launch derives from the name.

settings_payload.title: settings payload
settings_payload.description: The global, non-loadout settings of `protocol.json#/definitions/global_settings` — the whole object, never a delta, exactly as `msg_settings` carries it. Pushed on `pushWholeState()` (first paint, a launcher `init`, and a reloaded document per design/rendering-invariants.md §9a) and again whenever Rust pushes new settings down while the game runs, e.g. the player rebound the menu key in the launcher. It is **not** pushed as an echo of the page's own `setGlobal`: that call already returned what was stored, and re-pushing it would fight the control the player is holding — the same rule §6.5 sets for `setting` and `setModSetting`.

modaction_payload.$comment: **This event stops here. It is deliberately not forwarded to Rust, and `protocol.json`'s `v` is untouched by it.** The comparison to make is with `msg_hotkey`, whose `hotkey_id` stays a closed set of two globals (`loadout.next`, `overlay`). Those two are things Java has *already done* — the active loadout advanced, the menu opened — and the launcher has its own copy of that state, so its tray and its next launch would disagree with the running game if it were not told. A `modaction` is the opposite shape: it is a *request*, unfulfilled at the moment it is sent, and the thing that fulfils it is the page in the same JAR. The launcher holds no state that depends on whether a stopwatch is running, and a stopwatch that survived a relaunch is not a feature anyone asked for. Adding a third `hotkey_id` would have put a per-mod input vocabulary on a cross-process wire that has to stay compatible across launcher versions, to tell a process that has nothing to do about it.
modaction_payload.title: modaction payload
modaction_payload.description:
One mod-scoped key press, dispatched by Java for the page to act on.

The existing per-mod `keybind` hotkeys can say exactly one thing — flip this mod's `on` — and they say it by pushing `setting`. Java polls them from a table in `VoidClient.toggleMod`, edging each with `input/EdgeKey` against a code mirrored into `LiveState.applyActuatorFields`. That covers every mod whose key is a switch and no mod whose key is a verb, which is why `docs/mod-roster.md` §7 held Stopwatch back from the last wave: a `start_key` would have stored a key nothing acted on. This event is the second row of that table — same poll, same edge detection, same mirrored code — emitting a named action instead of writing a setting.

It is a notification and not a call: there is no return value and nothing is stored. Java has not changed any state by sending it, so a page that is not listening loses only the press. Deliver it in the frame the edge was seen; do not coalesce two presses of the same action into one, because two taps of a stopwatch's start key are a stop and a start.

mod.description: Which mod's key was pressed. The registry's own `mod_id` enum, `$ref`'d exactly as `setting_payload.id` refs it — the mod set is written down once, in `mods.json`, and a restated list here is a list that goes stale the next time a mod is added.

action.$comment: **A pattern, not a closed enum, and that is a decision rather than laziness.** The three closed sets nearby are closed because a consumer must handle them exhaustively: both shims build their channel map from `event_name`, so an undeclared channel is dropped in silence, and `void-core`'s `sync::pump` switches on `hotkey_id` to move the launcher's own pointer. Neither applies here. A `modaction` is dispatched by `mod` first, and the widget that owns that mod is the only code that reads the action — so an action nobody implements is a no-op inside one widget, not a lost channel. The two halves that must agree, the Java that edges the key and the widget that acts on it, ship in the same JAR as one binary, which is the same reason every payload on this surface is `additionalProperties: false`. And the vocabulary has no registry to derive from the way `mod_id` does: a closed enum here would be a fourth place a per-mod input is written down, after the mod's own settings prose, the Java table and the widget. Today it would be a closed set of two, invented for one mod. Revisit when three or four mods share a vocabulary — closing it then costs one enum and buys real exhaustiveness; closing it now buys a typo check on a string the same author writes on both sides.
action.description: What the key asked for: a short snake_case verb naming the *request*, never the key that made it. `start_stop`, not `bound_key`; `reset`, not `key_r`. Java knows which key is bound and the page must not care — a page that branched on key names would break the moment a player rebound one, and the same action can reach it from a keybind today and from a menu button tomorrow. The vocabulary is per mod and lives in that mod's own settings prose, which is where the Java wave and the page wave both read it: `stopwatch.start_key` names `start_stop` and `stopwatch.reset_key` names `reset`, and those two are the whole set today. An action the page does not recognise is ignored, not an error.

scoreboard_payload.$comment: **Whole state, pushed only on change.** Java reads the sidebar objective once a tick and compares it with the last push; a server that rewrites its board every second costs one envelope a second, and one that never changes costs nothing after the first. Older envelopes on the channel are dropped from the queue, as `keys` and `menu` are, because each one is the whole board. A reloaded page asks the sensor to forget what it sent, so the next tick resends it. Text is sent raw, `§` codes included: the page owns how a colour code is drawn, and the `scoreboard` mod's `server_colors` decides whether it is drawn at all.
scoreboard_payload.title: scoreboard payload
scoreboard_payload.description: The sidebar scoreboard, read the way `InGameHud#renderScoreboardObjective` reads it: the objective in the sidebar display slot, its scores sorted as vanilla sorts them, names starting with `#` dropped, the last fifteen kept, and each name decorated with its team prefix and suffix. `visible: false` when there is no sidebar objective — the page draws nothing then.

visible.description: Whether a sidebar objective is set.

title.description: The objective's display name, raw, `§` formatting codes included. Empty when `visible` is false.

lines.description: The lines top to bottom — highest score first, exactly the order vanilla draws them. At most fifteen.

text.description: The line as vanilla prints it: team prefix + player name + team suffix, raw, `§` codes included.

score.description: The line's score — the red number vanilla draws at the right edge.

call.title: Call
call.description: One JS to Java call, enveloped as {c, params}. In the real bridge `params` is the positional argument list of the method.

oneOf.description: Move or scale a HUD item.
Change one setting of one mod.
Pin mods to the quick panel.
Put text on the system clipboard.
Read text from the system clipboard.
Wear or take off one cosmetic.

call_result.title: Call result
call_result.description: The value one JS to Java call returned, enveloped as {c, returns}. Every call except `openKeybindCapture` returns synchronously, because the bridge is in-process (§6.5).

call_setGameplay.title: setGameplay call
call_setGameplay.description: `void.setGameplay(id, on)`. Writes the boolean field the mod's actuator Mixin reads every frame (§6.7). Synchronous and authoritative: the toggle in the UI shows the returned value, never an optimistic one.

items.description: Which gameplay mod to toggle. Only the five `kind: gameplay` mods are accepted; a HUD mod is a programming error.

setGameplay_returns.title: setGameplay returns
setGameplay_returns.description: The state actually applied. Normally equals the requested value; differs only if the mod refused the change.

result_setGameplay.title: setGameplay result
result_setGameplay.description: Envelope for a setGameplay return value.

call_setHud.title: setHud call
call_setHud.description: `void.setHud(id, placement)`. Called by the HUD editor on drop (§9). Java applies it to the live layout and mirrors the whole layout to Rust as the `hud` protocol message, which is what persists it.

items.description: The new placement. Same shape as a `hud_item` minus its `id`, which is the first argument.

anchor.description: Screen anchor the offsets are measured from.

dx.description: Horizontal offset in unscaled GUI pixels from the anchor.

dy.description: Vertical offset in unscaled GUI pixels from the anchor.

scale.description: Per-item size multiplier; omitted means leave unchanged.

setHud_returns.title: setHud returns
setHud_returns.description: The stored HUD item after snapping and clamping, so the editor can settle the dragged element on the value Java actually kept.

result_setHud.title: setHud result
result_setHud.description: Envelope for a setHud return value.

call_setModSetting.title: setModSetting call
call_setModSetting.description: `void.setModSetting(id, key, value)`. The generic writer behind every control in a mod's settings pane. The value must satisfy that mod's settings sub-schema in mods.json; Java clamps rather than throws when it does not.

items.description: Which mod to configure. Any of the 13.
Name of the setting, a property of that mod's settings sub-schema, e.g. `opacity`. `on` is settable here too, though gameplay mods should use `setGameplay`.
New value for the setting. Scalars only; no mod has an object- or array-valued setting.

setModSetting_returns.title: setModSetting returns
setModSetting_returns.description: The value actually stored, after clamping to the setting's range or enum. The control binds to this, not to what it sent.

result_setModSetting.title: setModSetting result
result_setModSetting.description: Envelope for a setModSetting return value.

call_setGlobal.title: setGlobal call
call_setGlobal.description: `void.setGlobal(key, value)`. The generic writer behind every control in the in-game Settings pane, and the exact mirror of `setModSetting` one level up: the loadout holds what changes how the game *plays*, and these are the globals of §8.3 that do not (`protocol.json#/definitions/global_settings`). Synchronous, like every call but `openKeybindCapture`, because the bridge is in-process. Java validates and clamps rather than throwing, stores the result, and returns **what it stored**; the control binds to that return value, never to what it sent. Java then reports the change to Rust, which is the store of record between sessions (§6.1) — the page does not persist anything itself.

items.description: Name of the global to write: a property of `protocol.json#/definitions/global_settings`, i.e. one of `menu_key`, `cycle_loadout_key`, `theme`, `ui_scale`, `hud_editor_grid`. Spelled as a pattern rather than an enum for the same reason `global_settings` is `additionalProperties: true` — the launcher may add a global without a protocol bump — and a key this build of Java does not know simply comes back `null`. The two that matter today are `menu_key` and `ui_scale`.

New value for the global. Scalars only; no global is object- or array-valued. `menu_key` and `cycle_loadout_key` take a `keybind` (mods.json validates the same names `openKeybindCapture` produces), `theme` a 1..32-character name, `ui_scale` a number clamped to 0.5..3, `hud_editor_grid` an integer clamped to 0..64.

setGlobal_returns.title: setGlobal returns
setGlobal_returns.description: The value actually stored, after validation and clamping — `null` when the key is not one Java knows, or when the value cannot be made usable (a `menu_key` that is not a legal key name, say). Null therefore means *nothing was stored*, so a control that gets it should keep showing the value it had. Exactly `setModSetting_returns`, one level up.

result_setGlobal.title: setGlobal result
result_setGlobal.description: Envelope for a setGlobal return value.

call_switchLoadout.title: switchLoadout call
call_switchLoadout.description: `void.switchLoadout(id)`. Writes every actuator field and re-renders the HUD in under a frame (§8.2), then reports `state` to Rust. A `loadout` event follows with the new loadout, so the caller does not need the returned object.

items.description: Id of a loadout present in the library Java received in `init.loadouts`.

switchLoadout_returns.title: switchLoadout returns
switchLoadout_returns.description: True when a loadout with that id existed and was applied; false when it did not, in which case nothing changed.

result_switchLoadout.title: switchLoadout result
result_switchLoadout.description: Envelope for a switchLoadout return value.

call_closeMenu.title: closeMenu call
call_closeMenu.description: `void.closeMenu()`. Closes VoidMenuScreen and returns the mouse to the game, the same thing the menu key does. A `menu` event with payload false follows.

closeMenu_returns.title: closeMenu returns
closeMenu_returns.description: Always null; the call has no result.

result_closeMenu.title: closeMenu result
result_closeMenu.description: Envelope for a closeMenu return value.

call_openKeybindCapture.title: openKeybindCapture call
call_openKeybindCapture.description: `void.openKeybindCapture(modId)`. The one asynchronous call on the bridge. It is still one synchronous hop like every other call, but the hop only **arms** the capture: Java answers `{c: 'openKeybindCapture', returns: null}` immediately, meaning "armed", and keeps key input until the player presses something. The key itself arrives later on the push channel, as a *call-result* envelope delivered through `__emit`: `__emit({c: 'openKeybindCapture', returns: 'V'})`, or `returns: null` when the player cancelled with Escape. The shim turns the armed answer into a pending Promise and the later envelope into its resolution, in FIFO order; the Promise never rejects. Because a null arrives on both channels, a shim must never read the synchronous null as the resolution — that is the one way to get this wrong. The captured key is not stored by this call; the UI writes it with `setModSetting(modId, 'key', captured)`.

items.description: The mod whose keybind is being captured, used only to label the capture prompt.

openKeybindCapture_returns.title: openKeybindCapture returns
openKeybindCapture_returns.description: Two different things travel in this shape, which is why it admits null twice over. The **synchronous** answer of `__void_native` is always null and means "capture armed". The **deferred** envelope, delivered later through `__emit`, carries the captured key — or null again when the player cancelled with Escape. A shim distinguishes them by channel, never by value: the synchronous answer opens a Promise, the `__emit` envelope resolves it.

oneOf.description: The captured key, delivered later through `__emit`.
Capture armed (the synchronous answer), or cancelled with Escape (the deferred one).

result_openKeybindCapture.title: openKeybindCapture result
result_openKeybindCapture.description: Envelope for an openKeybindCapture answer. Both the synchronous armed answer and the deferred resolution use it; only the channel tells them apart.

returns.description: Null when armed or cancelled; the captured key otherwise.

call_setSurfaces.title: setSurfaces call
call_setSurfaces.description: `void.setSurfaces(surfaces)`. Tells the host where the elements that carry an expensive effect are, so it can draw that effect in GL beneath the view instead. The overlay's CSS sets every `box-shadow` to `none` because a blurred shadow is the costliest thing a CPU rasteriser does; this is how the design keeps them anyway. The page sends the *authored* Figma values (the `--shadow-*-gl` tokens), so what the host draws is the design, not an approximation. Sent on layout change, not per frame.

setSurfaces_params.title: setSurfaces params
setSurfaces_params.description: [surfaces]. Replaces the whole set; an empty array clears it.

items.description: Every surface the host should draw an effect for.

effect_surface.title: Effect surface
effect_surface.description: One rectangle the host draws a shadow behind. Geometry is in CSS pixels of the view, the same space the page lays out in — the host scales by the device scale it already knows, so the page never has to reason about device pixels or the Retina factor.

id.description: Which surface this is, for logging. Not interpreted.

effect_shadow.title: Effect shadow
effect_shadow.description: A CSS `box-shadow` decomposed into numbers, so neither Java nor GLSL has to parse CSS. Taken from the authored `--shadow-*-gl` token, which the token build copies verbatim out of `design/tokens.css` — so this is the Figma value.

spread.description: Spread in CSS pixels; negative shrinks.

setSurfaces_returns.title: setSurfaces returns
setSurfaces_returns.description: How many surfaces the host kept, so the page can tell the call arrived.

result_setSurfaces.title: setSurfaces result
result_setSurfaces.description: Envelope for a setSurfaces return value.

toast_payload.$comment: Pushed by Java for things that happen with the menu closed, where nothing else on screen would say so: the loadout key cycled the loadout, the launcher switched or changed the library under the game, a mod's own key flipped it. Never pushed for a change the page made itself; the page raises its own notice for those (an import, a delete) without a round trip. Not coalesced, and not forwarded to Rust.
toast_payload.title: toast payload
toast_payload.description: One short notice, drawn over the game for a moment and then gone. Purely informational: nothing waits on it and nothing is lost if the page misses it.

kind.description: What the notice is about, so the page can pick its mark: `loadout` for a switch or a library change, `mod` for a mod a key flipped, `info` for anything else.

title.description: The main line, e.g. the loadout's name or `Fullbright on`.

detail.description: An optional second line, e.g. `Loadout switched`.

mod.description: For `kind: mod`, which mod. Lets the page draw the mod's own glyph.

call_createLoadout.title: createLoadout call
call_createLoadout.description: `void.createLoadout(name)`. Adds a loadout to the end of the library with every mod at its registry defaults and the factory HUD layout, and does not switch to it. Java picks the id (the name slugified, with a numeric suffix when taken) and tells Rust with `loadout_save`, which is what persists it. A `loadouts` event follows with the new library.

items.description: Display name. Trimmed; 1 to 48 characters after trimming.

createLoadout_returns.title: createLoadout returns
createLoadout_returns.description: The new loadout, or null when the name was empty or the library is full (128).

result_createLoadout.title: createLoadout result
result_createLoadout.description: Envelope for a createLoadout return value.

call_renameLoadout.title: renameLoadout call
call_renameLoadout.description: `void.renameLoadout(id, name)`. Changes a loadout's display name; the id is stable and does not follow it. Persisted with `loadout_save`; a `loadouts` event follows, and a `loadout` event too when the renamed loadout is the active one.

items.description: The new name. Trimmed; 1 to 48 characters after trimming.

renameLoadout_returns.title: renameLoadout returns
renameLoadout_returns.description: The name actually stored, after trimming, or null when the id is unknown or the name empty.

result_renameLoadout.title: renameLoadout result
result_renameLoadout.description: Envelope for a renameLoadout return value.

call_duplicateLoadout.title: duplicateLoadout call
call_duplicateLoadout.description: `void.duplicateLoadout(id)`. Appends a copy of a loadout, mods, settings, HUD layout and quick pins, named `<name> copy`, with no stats. Does not switch to it. Persisted with `loadout_save`; a `loadouts` event follows.

duplicateLoadout_returns.title: duplicateLoadout returns
duplicateLoadout_returns.description: The copy, or null when the id is unknown or the library is full.

result_duplicateLoadout.title: duplicateLoadout result
result_duplicateLoadout.description: Envelope for a duplicateLoadout return value.

call_deleteLoadout.title: deleteLoadout call
call_deleteLoadout.description: `void.deleteLoadout(id)`. Removes a loadout from the library. Refused for the last one. When it was the active loadout, the first remaining one is applied exactly as a switch is, and a `loadout` event follows. Persisted with `loadout_delete`; a `loadouts` event follows.

deleteLoadout_returns.title: deleteLoadout returns
deleteLoadout_returns.description: True when the loadout was deleted; false when the id was unknown or it was the last one.

result_deleteLoadout.title: deleteLoadout result
result_deleteLoadout.description: Envelope for a deleteLoadout return value.

call_exportLoadout.title: exportLoadout call
call_exportLoadout.description: `void.exportLoadout(id)`. Encodes a loadout as a share code: `VOID1.` + base64url (no padding) of the raw-DEFLATE-compressed UTF-8 JSON of the loadout's name, icon, server, mc, registry version, HUD layout, quick pins and *only the settings that differ from the registry defaults*, then `.` + the CRC-32 of that JSON as 8 lowercase hex digits. Ids and stats are never in a code. The same format is produced and read by `void_loadout::share` in Rust and `ShareCode` in Java; `schema/share-code.fixtures.json` holds codes each side made, and both test suites decode all of them.

exportLoadout_returns.title: exportLoadout returns
exportLoadout_returns.description: The share code, or null when the id is unknown.

result_exportLoadout.title: exportLoadout result
result_exportLoadout.description: Envelope for a exportLoadout return value.

call_importLoadout.title: importLoadout call
call_importLoadout.description: `void.importLoadout(code)`. Decodes a share code and appends the loadout it carries to the library under a fresh id, without switching to it. Structure is strict: an unknown version, a bad checksum, undecodable data or a missing name refuses the whole code. Content is lenient: a mod or setting this build does not know, or a value outside its schema range, is dropped (the mod falls back to its default) and counted in `dropped`, so a code made on a newer client still imports. The result is a valid `loadout.json` loadout. Persisted with `loadout_save`; a `loadouts` event follows.

items.description: The share code as pasted. Surrounding whitespace is ignored.

result_importLoadout.title: importLoadout result
result_importLoadout.description: Envelope for a importLoadout return value.

loadout.description: The imported loadout, as now stored in the library.

dropped.description: Settings, mods, HUD items and pins the code carried that this build could not use.

error.description: Why the code was refused: `empty` nothing was pasted; `format` it is not a share code or its data does not decode; `version` it was made by a newer format; `checksum` it was damaged in transit; `invalid` it decoded but carries no usable loadout; `full` the library already holds 128.

call_setQuickPins.title: setQuickPins call
call_setQuickPins.description: `void.setQuickPins(ids)`. Replaces the active loadout's quick-panel pins (`loadout.json#/definitions/quick_pins`). Unknown and repeated ids are dropped and the list is cut to eight. Persisted with `loadout_save`; nothing is pushed back, the return is the stored list.

result_setQuickPins.title: setQuickPins result
result_setQuickPins.description: Envelope for a setQuickPins return value.

call_setClipboard.title: setClipboard call
call_setClipboard.description: `void.setClipboard(text)`. Puts plain text on the system clipboard — what the Loadouts screen's `Copy code` does with a share code. Why the bridge carries a clipboard at all: the Ultralight binding implements no platform clipboard, so Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V do nothing inside the in-game page and `navigator.clipboard` does not exist there. A share code is a line of text a player has to get out of the game and into Discord, and back. Java owns the system clipboard (`Screen.setClipboard` / `getClipboard`), so the page asks it.

setClipboard_returns.title: setClipboard returns
setClipboard_returns.description: True when the host put it on the clipboard.

result_setClipboard.title: setClipboard result
result_setClipboard.description: Envelope for a setClipboard return value.

call_getClipboard.title: getClipboard call
call_getClipboard.description: `void.getClipboard()`. The system clipboard's plain text, for the Loadouts screen's `Paste code`. Empty when the clipboard holds no text or cannot be read. Only ever called on a click, never polled.

getClipboard_returns.title: getClipboard returns
getClipboard_returns.description: The clipboard's text, cut to 16384 characters; empty when there is none.

result_getClipboard.description: Envelope for a getClipboard return value.

payload.description: The local player's set, what they own, and the catalog version.
The emote now playing, or null when it ended.

cosmetics_payload.title: cosmetics payload
cosmetics_payload.description: What the in-game wardrobe needs: the local player's whole equipped set, every item the account owns, and the version of the catalog this jar was built with. Whole state, so a newer one in the same frame replaces an older one. Pushed on `pushWholeState()` (first paint, a launcher `init`, a reloaded document) and whenever the launcher changes either half underneath the game — a `cosmetics` message after an equip from the launcher Store, or a purchase landing. **Not** pushed as an echo of the page's own `equipCosmetic`, `setCosmeticTint` or `setEmoteWheel`: each of those already returned what was stored, and §6.5 does not push a change back to the page that made it.

self.description: What the local player wears — `protocol.json`'s `equipped_set`, the same object the launcher sends in `cosmetics.self`, so the wardrobe and the wire cannot disagree about its shape.

owned.description: Every item the account owns, free items included, in catalog order. An item not listed shows as locked; equipping it is refused.

catalog_version.description: `cosmetics.json#/version` as compiled into this jar. The page's catalog is generated from the same file, so a mismatch means the bundle and the jar were not built together.

emote_payload.title: emote payload
emote_payload.description: The local player's emote started (`id`) or ended (`null`), so the wheel can light the one playing and the HUD can step aside for the third-person camera. Not coalesced: a start and an end in one slow frame are two facts, and the page should see both in order. The start is **not** pushed when the page's own `playEmote` started it — that call returned `true` and is the notification — but the end always is, because only Java knows when a clip finishes or is cancelled by movement.

id.description: The emote now playing, or null when none is.

cosmetic_tint.title: Cosmetic tint
cosmetic_tint.description: A per-slot recolour, `#rrggbb`. The same pattern `protocol.json`'s `equipped_set.tints` uses; Java accepts either case and answers lower case.

call_equipCosmetic.title: equipCosmetic call
call_equipCosmetic.description: `void.equipCosmetic(slot, id)`. Wears `id` in `slot`, or takes the slot off when `id` is null. Applied in Java at once — the next frame draws it — and forwarded to the launcher as an `equip` protocol message, which persists it to the backend. Java refuses only what it can see is wrong: an id the catalog does not know, an item for another slot, or one it knows the account does not own. When it does not know what the account owns, the backend validates and the launcher reverts a refused equip with a `cosmetics` message, which reaches the page as a `cosmetics` event. Synchronous and authoritative like every call here: an item the account does not own, an id the catalog does not know, or an item for another slot is **refused**, and the answer is then what the slot still holds. Bind the wardrobe to the return, never to what was sent. No `cosmetics` event follows.

items.description: The item to wear, or null to take the slot off.

equipCosmetic_returns.title: equipCosmetic returns
equipCosmetic_returns.description: The id now worn in that slot, or null when it is empty. Equals the request on success; on a refusal it is whatever was already there.

result_equipCosmetic.title: equipCosmetic result
result_equipCosmetic.description: Envelope for a equipCosmetic return value.

returns.description: The id worn in that slot now.

call_setCosmeticTint.title: setCosmeticTint call
call_setCosmeticTint.description: `void.setCosmeticTint(slot, hex)`. Recolours the item worn in `slot`, or clears the tint when `hex` is null. Only items flagged `tintable` in `cosmetics.json` take one; for any other slot the call is refused and answers the tint already set. Applied in game only for now: the wire's `equip` carries a slot and an id, not a tint, so a tint chosen here lasts the session until the protocol grows one. No `cosmetics` event follows.

items.description: The colour, `#rrggbb`, or null to clear it.

setCosmeticTint_returns.title: setCosmeticTint returns
setCosmeticTint_returns.description: The tint now applied, lower case, or null when the slot has none.

result_setCosmeticTint.title: setCosmeticTint result
result_setCosmeticTint.description: Envelope for a setCosmeticTint return value.

call_setEmoteWheel.title: setEmoteWheel call
call_setEmoteWheel.description: `void.setEmoteWheel(ids)`. Replaces the whole emote wheel. Ids that are not emotes, are not owned, or repeat are dropped, and the wheel keeps at most eight. Applied in game only for now: the wire has no message for the wheel, so it lasts the session until the protocol grows one; the launcher Store edits the stored wheel. No `cosmetics` event follows.

setEmoteWheel_returns.title: setEmoteWheel returns
setEmoteWheel_returns.description: The wheel as stored, after dropping what could not be kept.

result_setEmoteWheel.title: setEmoteWheel result
result_setEmoteWheel.description: Envelope for a setEmoteWheel return value.

call_playEmote.title: playEmote call
call_playEmote.description: `void.playEmote(id)`. Starts an emote for the local player and tells the launcher, which relays it to the other VOID players on the server as a remote `emote`. Refused — `false`, and nothing plays — for an id that is not an emote, is not owned, or has no bundled animation. The `emote` event's start is not pushed for a call that succeeded, since this answer is the notification; its end is.

playEmote_returns.title: playEmote returns
playEmote_returns.description: True when the emote started; false when it was refused.

result_playEmote.title: playEmote result
result_playEmote.description: Envelope for a playEmote return value.
